Liver Disease in Pregnancy

normal pregnancy liver tests · the gestational age clock · placental alkaline phosphatase · bile acids · acute fatty liver vs hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets (HELLP)Which liver disease fits this week of pregnancy, and is the pregnancy causing it at all?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Gestational age sorts it: vomiting from 5 to 18 weeks is hyperemesis gravidarum; itching in the 2nd or 3rd trimester is intrahepatic cholestasis; after 20 weeks with hemolysis and low platelets is HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets); near term, liver failure is acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP).
  • An isolated alkaline phosphatase rise, up to 2 to 3 times normal at term with normal AST, ALT and bilirubin, is placental: reassure.
  • HELLP and AFLP are treated by delivery; intrahepatic cholestasis gets ursodeoxycholic acid and delivery at 37 weeks.
What it is

Liver test changes in pregnancy: physiologic (placental alkaline phosphatase), pregnancy-specific (hyperemesis, intrahepatic cholestasis, HELLP, AFLP) or unrelated to pregnancy (viral hepatitis, the most common cause of jaundice).

Driver

A different driver for each: hormone-driven bile stasis, a fatty acid oxidation defect, endothelial injury with platelet activation, or vomiting.

Triggers

Maternal LCHAD (long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase) variant: AFLP risk 20 times higher

non-modifiable

; cholestasis in an earlier pregnancy

non-modifiable

; ancestry from Bolivia or Chile

non-modifiable

; twins or a molar pregnancy behind hyperemesis

non-modifiable

; oral contraceptives bring the itch back

Chain

Pregnancy estrogen and progesterone

normal bile stasis is exaggerated and bile excretion falls

serum bile acids rise

intense itching; preterm birth and stillbirth risk

Insights

Only alkaline phosphatase rises in a normal pregnancy, because the placenta makes it; a raised AST, ALT or bilirubin is disease.

Ursodeoxycholic acid eases the itch and the labs but does not lower fetal complications, so the timing of delivery protects the fetus.

Pause point. Bait: a raised alkaline phosphatase late in pregnancy looks cholestatic; with no itching, normal bile acids and normal AST, ALT and bilirubin, it is placental.

Risk and timing
FindingMeaning
Bile acids above 40 micromol/LFetal demise more likely
Bile acids 100 micromol/L or moreDeliver at 36 weeks (step 7)
HELLP at 34 weeks or moreDeliver now, after stabilizing

7Treatment
1

First lineIntrahepatic cholestasis

Ursodeoxycholic acid for the itch and the labs; deliver at 37 weeks, or at 36 weeks when bile acids are 100 micromol/L or more. In practice: the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists times delivery at 36 to 39 weeks when bile acids are under 100 micromol/L.

2

DeliveryHELLP syndrome

Magnesium sulfate against seizures and antihypertensives, then delivery; under 34 weeks and stable, corticosteroids first.

3

DeliveryAcute fatty liver of pregnancy

Prompt delivery is usually advised, or ending the pregnancy, depending on gestational age.

4

SupportHyperemesis gravidarum

IV fluids, electrolytes and antiemetics such as the antihistamine dimenhydrinate; thiamine before any dextrose.

8Follow-up
After delivery
SituationDo
After intrahepatic cholestasisItching usually settles within about 48 h of delivery; expect it again in later pregnancies and on oral contraceptives.
After AFLPTest mother and infant for LCHAD variants; survivors recover fully without recurrence.
After HELLP or preeclampsiaWatch for postpartum onset, most often within 4 days and up to 6 weeks.
Practice
  1. 26 yo F at 34 weeks with intense palmar pruritus, raised bile acids and no rash → Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy → ursodeoxycholic acid
  2. 26 yo F at 36 weeks with hypoglycemia, coagulopathy and raised transaminases → Acute fatty liver of pregnancy → urgent delivery
  3. 26 yo F at 34 weeks with hypertension, hemolysis, high LFTs and platelets 68,000 → HELLP syndrome → delivery
  4. 26 yo F at 9 weeks with intractable vomiting, ketonuria and mildly raised transaminases → Hyperemesis gravidarum
  5. 26 yo F at 14 weeks, obese with diabetes and raised transaminases → Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease – the third-trimester diseases do not fit at 14 weeks
  6. 26 yo F at 30 weeks with an isolated alkaline phosphatase twice normal, all else normal → Placental alkaline phosphatase – physiologic → reassurance
  7. 26 yo F at 34 weeks with intractable palmar pruritus and raised bile acids, taking ursodeoxycholic acid → Delivery at 36 to 37 weeks → intrahepatic cholestasis carries stillbirth risk
  8. 29 yo F at 35 weeks with hypoglycemia, coagulopathy, raised ammonia and rising creatinine → Emergent delivery → acute fatty liver of pregnancy is treated by delivering
  9. 28 yo F at 32 weeks with alkaline phosphatase three times normal on routine labs; AST, ALT and bilirubin normal; no symptoms → Reassurance → the placenta makes alkaline phosphatase
Alkaline phosphatase in pregnancy Alkaline phosphatase normally rises in pregnancy because the placenta makes its own isoenzyme; levels run 2–4× normal. AST (aspartate aminotransferase), ALT (alanine aminotransferase) and bilirubin do not rise physiologically; any elevation is pathologic.

AFLP vs. HELLP Hypoglycemia, coagulopathy, high ammonia and renal failure indicate AFLP (acute fatty liver of pregnancy). Hemolysis, thrombocytopenia and more hypertension indicate HELLP (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) syndrome. Both are treated by delivering. Cholecystectomy in pregnancy is safest in the second trimester.
Transferable rule Before diagnosing a pregnancy-specific liver disease, check that the gestational age fits it.
